extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants and mentors (K awards, R01/R03/R21/R35, F/K fellowships) and research PIs seeking practical funding/process guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical Q&A and procedural guidance about NIH grant submission, review, paylines, Program Officer interactions, JITs, resubmissions (A0/A1), K-award rules, and award timing under budget/CR conditions. Targeted at applicants preparing or awaiting NIH decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission timing relative to Summary Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Summary Statement has been released then you can submit the exact same app or a different one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start writing once the Summary Statement is out; if the science is very different you could have sent a different application before the SS was released. Wait for the SS to decide whether to rework or resubmit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program Officer disclosure and job‑market activity
rubrics_metrics.description: If you tell your PO that you are looking for faculty jobs, you might not be considered for an award; ICs feel that if you are ready for the job market you do not need the additional postdoc training on the K99.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not actively apply for or publicly represent yourself as 'on the job market' before award decisions; you can quietly keep an eye out but when asked by a PO about applying, say no if you are not actually submitting applications. POs may be strict about funding applicants they believe are leaving training.

rubrics_metrics.name: K99 phase minimum duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The K99 phase needs to last at least 1 year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions can delay hiring until after the K99 (if willing to postpone start) so having one full year of K99 is sufficient for many hires.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH rule on reducing or skipping the K99 phase
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH stopped allowing skipping or reducing the K99 time (i.e., eliminating or shortening the mentored K99 portion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although applicants may try to negotiate reduced K99 time if offered a faculty position, NIH policy prevents skipping/reducing the K99 portion; plan for the full mentored period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent K award and RPG (e.g., K23 and R01) policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If you receive an R01 in the first 3 years of your K23, you will lose your K23; you can only hold both awards during the final 2 years of a K23.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is NIH policy (see NOT-OD-18-157). It is not about percent effort — the intent is that K awardees focus on training for at least 3 years. You may submit an R01 earlier and relinquish the K if funded, but this may harm future relationships with the IC that funded your K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paylines depend on IC and mechanism; percentiles/impact scores determine fundability
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding depends on the IC, mechanism, and paylines (percentile or impact score). Percentiles are used to compare across study sections; impact scores can be used to predict percentiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism-specific and IC-specific paylines vary (e.g., NICHD discretionary zones, NIGMS vs NCI differences). A strong improvement in score bodes well; still, you don't know for certain until NOA. Small analyses may predict percentile from impact score (example formula shown), but many variables affect outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council review timing and award processing
rubrics_metrics.description: After receiving your score you typically wait until after the next Council meeting; award processing and timing (e.g., NOA issuance) follow Council and the federal budget timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a multi-month lag between impact score and award decision (example: Council in January may yield awards around April 1). POs can give more precise next-step guidance only after Summary Statement and Council timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal budget / Continuing Resolution (CR) effects on award decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: ICs commonly wait for the federal budget to be signed into law before making awards; CRs and budget uncertainty delay award processing and PO certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During a CR ICs may be reluctant to commit funds; final paylines are retroactive once appropriation is known. Award timing can be delayed months until the FY appropriation is decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to contact your Program Officer (PO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact your PO after you receive the Summary Statement for next steps; POs can advise whether to resubmit or how likely funding is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be respectful of PO time; they may not respond immediately during budget/CR chaos. If PO asks for a brief response or guidance, comply; otherwise wait for them or GMS to request further materials (e.g., JIT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Just‑In‑Time (JIT) submission practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not proactively submit JIT materials; wait for the automatic/explicit JIT request from NIH (PO or GMS will contact you when ready to process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NIH/GMS will request JIT items (current other support, visa paperwork, etc.) when processing is appropriate. Submitting JIT without request is unnecessary and may not help.

rubrics_metrics.name: A0 vs A1 resubmission strategy and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmitting (A1) can improve score; many ICs may still fund the A0 even if the A1 score drops, but some ICs (e.g., NCI) place more emphasis on the A1 and might penalize the A0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss resubmission plans with your PO. An improved A1 score can sometimes accelerate funding of the earlier A0. Follow PO advice on whether to resubmit (often suggested if score is borderline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism- and FOA-specific funding zones
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding lines and the meaning of a given score/percentile depend on the grant mechanism (R03, R21, R15, R35, K awards, F fellowships) and the FOA/IC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret your score in context: e.g., some mechanisms are not percentiled (PARs), some ICs historically have different paylines (NIGMS vs NCI vs NICHD). Ask your PO what funding likelihood is given your mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary and secondary IC assignment and transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not have a secondary IC assigned it is too late to add one after review; transferring to another IC requires the primary IC to relinquish the application and the receiving IC to accept it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can contact a secondary IC PO to gauge interest; if the secondary IC is willing, the primary IC must formally release the application. Many ICs do not fund secondary assignments, so this is not guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: IC discretion and select-pay (out‑of‑order) decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: ICs can exercise discretionary or select-pay decisions (pick applications out of order) for RFAs or special programs; this affects funding unpredictably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For RFAs or special initiatives POs may recommend applications for select pay; for standard RFAs/FOAs funding order can differ from strict score order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of existing/other support on funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: High levels of other funding or overlap with another award can be a reason for skipping an application even with a low percentile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose other support appropriately; internal funding that can be repurposed might affect timing/budget questions but not necessarily the chance of funding. POs consider overall portfolio and overlaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program Officer advocacy and language
rubrics_metrics.description: PO statements like 'cautiously optimistic' are the closest indication a PO can give about likelihood of funding (pending administrative review and budget).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat PO conservatism as normal; a 'cautiously optimistic' PO usually signals a reasonable chance but not a guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑award spending rules
rubrics_metrics.description: You may spend (or set up a pre‑award account) up to 90 days before the NOA is issued if your institution allows pre‑award spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to spend in advance, discuss with your grants office and GMS timelines; contacting GMS (not PO) can give a time estimate once JIT submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to PO requests for brief rebuttals or responses
rubrics_metrics.description: A PO may request a brief response (e.g., 1–2 pages) to reviewers' comments as part of internal consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit concise, focused responses when asked; lack of further comment from PO after your response often implies no immediate concerns and that you can wait on funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting 'no response' from PO
rubrics_metrics.description: PO silence does not necessarily indicate negative news — often it means the PO is waiting for budget decisions or is busy; 'no news is good news' can apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you haven't heard by a reasonable later date (e.g., early–mid January for winter cycles), a polite follow-up to ask whether you should prepare to resubmit is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile retroactivity and final paylines
rubrics_metrics.description: Final paylines are retroactive once the FY appropriation is known; interim paylines may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application falling within historic final paylines may still be funded once final appropriations are set even if interim paylines appear less favorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applications without percentiles (PARs) using impact scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mechanisms (e.g., PARs) do not yield percentiles; impact factors/scores can be used to approximate funding likelihood and compare across prior data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can analyze impact scores vs percentiles from historical data to estimate funding chances, but caution is needed because mechanisms/ICs vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI status and exceptions for award length
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to typical R01 durations (e.g., 5 years vs 4 years) are sometimes made for Early Stage Investigators (ESIs) and clinical trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting 5 years does not guarantee 5 years of funding; ICs must manage average RPG lengths and may limit most R01s to 4 years except in justified cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical JIT content and procedural steps during award processing
rubrics_metrics.description: GMS/JIT requests can include visa support, current other support, and other administrative documentation required for award issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond promptly to JIT requests; these are routine steps in award processing and often precede administrative review and NOA preparation.
